items.title: [pv-magazine.com] IEA projects India’s renewable capacity will reach 530 GW by 2030
items.content_html: India’s installed renewable power capacity is forecast to reach about 530 gigawatts by 2030, including more than 350 GW of solar, according to an International Energy Agency (IEA) report released Saturday. Globally, the agency forecasts nearly 4,800 GW of renewable capacity additions from 2026 to 2031, driven increasingly by governments seeking to limit exposure to imported fuels and price shocks. Solar is expected to account for more than 80% of India’s renewable capacity growth through 2030. The IEA projects renewable generation will rise from about 500 terawatt-hours in 2025 to roughly 950 TWh in 2030. Rooftop and other solar capacity for self-consumption will also grow as commercial, industrial and household installations expand. The forecast depends on faster investment in transmission and storage, more flexible power systems and improvements in distribution companies’ finances. Land acquisition and project delays also threaten delivery. The IEA said addressing these barriers could raise India’s renewable additions in 2026–2030 by more than 20% above its main forecast.

items.title: [euronews.com] Early Arctic vortex disruption raises cold risk; climate link remains unproven
items.content_html: Meteorologists are tracking an unusually early weakening of the Arctic polar vortex, a circulation high above the pole. Its disruption can shift atmospheric patterns and increase the chance of cold outbreaks across parts of Europe, North America and Asia. The event is occurring in early November, weeks or months before major disruptions usually develop. Its effects may take weeks to reach weather systems near the surface. Climate change has been suggested as a possible influence on the atmospheric processes involved, but researchers have not established a direct link to this event, and the proposed connection remains disputed. Scientists are also assessing the influence of a strong El Niño and natural variability. The weather effects depend on how the disturbance develops and interacts with other atmospheric systems.

items.title: [oilprice.com] U.S. nuclear expansion faces uranium conversion and enrichment shortfalls
items.content_html: U.S. nuclear expansion faces constraints in uranium fuel processing: foreign suppliers provided 93% of the uranium delivered to U.S. reactors, and only five plants worldwide convert uranium at scale. The West needs about 44,000 metric tons of uranium feedstock a year but has capacity for roughly 34,000 tons, according to figures cited by Oilprice.com. Urenco USA’s New Mexico plant supplies about a third of U.S. enrichment demand, and the company says its expansion is ahead of schedule and on budget. Russia accounts for nearly half of global enrichment capacity. Uranium enrichment also requires electricity, while technology companies are seeking reliable electricity supplies and increasingly turning to nuclear power.

items.title: [scimex.org] Heatwave feedback can add 10% to extreme temperatures, study finds
items.content_html: A study led by Yinglin Tian, a scientist at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, found that interactions among heat, dry soils and high atmospheric pressure can make the most extreme mid-latitude heatwaves about 10% hotter. High pressure brings more sunlight to the surface, while dry soils provide less evaporative cooling. In Central Europe, the threshold for this feedback is about 29°C; the chance of crossing it rose from 6% in 1979–83 to 23% in 2018–22. The researchers used machine learning and statistical analysis to identify the process, which they say current heat forecasting models do not represent well. A separate study led by Freie Universität Berlin researcher Philipp Aglas-Leitner compared 22 exceptional heatwaves from 2010–23 with projections through 2100. It found that future events could last longer and affect larger areas. For many regions, most model ensembles project at least one exceptional heatwave period a year in 2060–99.

items.title: [phys.org] UN warns warming will breach 1.5C as COP31 opens Monday
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The United Nations says global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold as nearly 200 countries prepare to begin the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9. Climate scientists say the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to become the second year to exceed 1.5C, after 2024. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the world must now limit how far temperatures rise beyond that level and blamed political leaders for failing to act. The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

items.title: [fuelcellsworks.com] Google confirms $17 billion Wyoming campus with 702MW gas fuel cells
items.content_html: Google confirmed on Nov. 5 that it will invest $17 billion in its first Wyoming data center near Cheyenne, supported by a planned 702-megawatt natural-gas fuel-cell plant with carbon capture and storage. Bloom Energy will supply the fuel cells, and the captured carbon dioxide is intended for underground storage at Tallgrass Energy’s Eastern Wyoming hub. Natural-gas generators operated by Tallgrass and Black Hills Energy will supplement the fuel-cell plant. Google says it will cover the full cost of its electricity and the infrastructure required directly by the campus. The capture system is still planned, and AEP, which announced the fuel-cell project, has not disclosed a guaranteed capture rate. Construction of the fuel-cell facility is expected to begin in 2026, with full operation by the end of 2028. The campus is slated for completion in 2031.

items.title: [energynow.com] AI power demand drives microgrid investment and grid planning
items.content_html: The expansion of artificial-intelligence data centers is increasing electricity demand and accelerating investment in microgrids, grid upgrades and new power arrangements in the United States, the Gulf and Southeast Asia. U.S. microgrid-market revenue is forecast to rise from $8 billion in 2025 to $21.2 billion by 2030, according to GlobalData. In Abu Dhabi, state-owned energy company ADNOC, OpenAI and technology group G42 announced a partnership to apply AI across energy operations. ADNOC says an initial project will combine records from thousands of wells and hundreds of facilities to speed development planning, although the projected gains have not been independently demonstrated. In Southeast Asia, the World Economic Forum says data-center plans are outpacing local grid capacity, while the region needs power links and renewable-energy trading infrastructure. The POWERGEN 2027 conference, scheduled for Jan. 18-21 in Salt Lake City, will bring together utility, grid and security executives to discuss demand growth, reliability, cybersecurity and AI.

items.title: [koreaherald.com] South Korea forecasts warmer, wetter winter as record El Niño persists
items.content_html: South Korea’s weather agency forecast a warmer, wetter winter on the Korean Peninsula as a record-strength El Niño continues to influence weather patterns. The Korea Meteorological Administration said temperatures in November, December and January are likely to exceed long-term averages, with more rain than usual in November and December. It also warned that cold spells remain possible. The agency said the average sea-surface temperature in the Pacific monitoring region from August through October was 2.4°C above normal, the highest for that period since records began in 1950. The event may also affect global annual temperatures, but forecasts differ: Berkeley Earth puts the chance that 2026 will be the warmest year on record at 96%, while the U.S. National Centers for Environmental Information puts it at 0.1% and gives the year an 86.9% chance of ranking second. Scientists say El Niño’s warming influence comes from heat accumulated in the ocean, much of it linked to greenhouse-gas emissions. Its largest effect on global temperatures is expected in 2027. Recent storms in the Southwest killed at least four people, and Clovis, New Mexico, recorded 28.84 inches of rain since Sept. 20, compared with a historical average of 3.3 inches.

items.title: [rte.ie] COP31 set to open in Türkiye with fossil-fuel and finance disputes
items.content_html: Nearly 200 countries are due to begin the U.N. COP31 climate talks in Antalya on Nov. 9, with negotiations scheduled to run through Nov. 20 and more than 100,000 participants expected. Türkiye will host while Australia leads negotiations under a compromise over the summit’s location. The conference will focus on implementing earlier climate pledges rather than agreeing on new targets. The agenda includes Türkiye’s push to raise electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035, preferably using renewable power, and efforts to include electrification in the summit’s final political statement. Disputes are expected over stronger language on phasing out fossil fuels and whether wealthy countries will provide more funding for developing nations adapting to climate impacts. Türkiye’s environment minister and COP31 president, Murat Kurum, says the summit should turn previous commitments into results. The European Union wants electrification explicitly described as “clean,” while African negotiators are pressing to add a pledge to triple adaptation finance to the agenda. The Trump administration will not take part in the negotiations, although a U.S. congressional delegation is expected to attend.

items.title: [e360.yale.edu] Super El Niño drought threatens crops and deepens global food insecurity
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A powerful El Niño is worsening drought in several food-producing regions. The United Nations World Food Programme warns that it could push 49 million more people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, bringing the total to 274 million. Drought has already cut rainfall in northern Sudan to less than half of normal, while dry conditions are affecting crops, livestock and transport in parts of Central America and Southeast Asia. The Famine Early Warning Systems Network projects that 2026-27 production of maize, wheat and rice will be 2.7% below the previous year but still the second-largest on record. El Niño is forecast to peak in December and persist into early 2027. In the Philippines, forecasters expect below-normal rainfall in November and drought conditions in several provinces.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s seasonal outlook favors wetter conditions across much of the southern United States through February 2027 as a strong El Niño develops. Warm Pacific waters can increase atmospheric moisture, while recent rain left rivers high and soils saturated in parts of the Southwest, worsening runoff when further storms arrived. The winter’s snowpack remains uncertain; Colorado climatologist Russ Schumacher said rainfall could help the Colorado River’s reservoirs but would not reverse their decline.

items.title: [carbonbrief.org] Brazil adds country-readiness test to fossil-fuel roadmap ahead of COP31
items.content_html: Brazil’s presidency of the 30th U.N. climate conference (COP30) has outlined a voluntary “Belém readiness” assessment in its roadmap for shifting away from coal, oil and gas. The assessment asks countries to examine their exposure to fossil fuels and capacity to transition across energy demand, energy supply and the wider economy, then choose policies suited to their circumstances. The framework is due for discussion at the 31st U.N. climate conference (COP31) in Antalya on Nov. 10, but Brazil says it is guidance for action, not a text for negotiation. COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago said implementation should involve finance, transport, energy and infrastructure ministries, not just climate negotiators. Joeri Rogelj, a professor of climate science and policy at Imperial College London, said the roadmap lacks a clear pace of change and benchmarks for assessing progress toward the Paris Agreement’s temperature goals. Climate advocates have called for governments to turn the framework into commitments with timelines and resources.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN warns climate adaptation funding leaves vulnerable countries exposed
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report says developing countries remain exposed to worsening floods, droughts and heat because adaptation funding is not reaching vulnerable communities at the scale required. Least-developed countries and small island states need an estimated $40 billion to $50 billion annually, equivalent to 3% to 4% of their gross domestic product, while support to least-developed countries fell 16% from 2022 to 2024. Adaptation measures include flood barriers, heat-resistant hospitals and drought-resilient water and farming systems. Low- and middle-income countries accounted for 99% of the 765 million people affected by floods and landslides between 2020 and 2025. Communities also face obstacles to turning plans into projects, including weak institutional coordination and difficulty accessing funding for climate-related losses. At the COP31 climate conference, opening in Antalya on Nov. 9, campaigners are urging governments to set out a concrete funding plan and prioritize grants or concessional loans over high-interest borrowing for projects that generate little direct revenue. Concessional loans are easier to repay than high-interest loans.

items.title: [climatechangenews.com] Brazil sets voluntary timetable for global shift from fossil fuels
items.content_html: Brazil’s presidency of the COP30 climate summit published a 182-page voluntary roadmap on Nov. 3 to help countries move away from coal, oil and gas, proposing a staged process through 2033. It asks governments to prepare national plans by 2028, build clean-energy systems and supporting infrastructure through 2030, then focus on adjusting fossil-fuel supply from 2031 to 2033. The guide does not assign obligations to individual countries or set binding phaseout targets; it offers a framework for governments to assess their circumstances and choose measures. Brazil says it is meant to help governments implement existing climate agreements. COP31 opens in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9, and the roadmap is scheduled for discussion there on Nov. 10.
